name: Table Formats and the Lakehouse
intent: Put database-like tables on cheap object storage by tracking files in versioned metadata and committing changes with one atomic pointer swap.
scenario: An orders table lives as Parquet files in an object store (cheap file storage such as S3). Two streaming writers append micro-batches (small groups of rows) to it while analysts query it. Without a table format, a reader can see half a write and a writer can overwrite another's work. With one, each commit is an atomic snapshot and a lost race simply retries.
problem: A directory of Parquet files is not a table. Object stores have no transactions and no rename that is atomic for many files, so a reader can list a half-finished write, two writers can clobber each other, a failed job leaves stray files, and a query has to list thousands of objects to learn what the table contains. You also cannot update or delete one row without rewriting whole files, and you cannot ask what the table looked like yesterday.

howItWorks.title: Data files are immutable
howItWorks.text: Rows live in columnar files (Parquet, ORC) that are written once and never modified. An update or delete writes new files, and either rewrites the affected files (copy-on-write) or adds small delete files that are merged at read time (merge-on-read). Immutability is what makes snapshots and time travel cheap.

howItWorks.title: Metadata says which files are the table
howItWorks.text: A snapshot is a list of data files, kept in manifest files with per-file stats: row counts and min/max per column. In Iceberg a metadata file points to a manifest list, which points to manifests, which point to data files. Delta Lake keeps an ordered JSON transaction log with periodic checkpoints. Hudi keeps a timeline. The table is whatever the latest snapshot lists, not whatever sits in the bucket.

howItWorks.title: A commit is one atomic pointer swap
howItWorks.text: A writer uploads its data files first, then writes new manifests and a new metadata file, and finally asks the catalog (the service that stores each table's current pointer: Hive metastore, REST catalog, Glue, or a conditional put on an object) to move the table pointer from the version it started from to the new one, only if nothing changed. Until that swap, nothing is visible, so readers never see a partial write.

howItWorks.title: Concurrency is optimistic
howItWorks.text: If the swap fails because another writer won, the loser re-reads the new head and validates: appends commute and can be replayed, but a rewrite of a file that someone else already replaced is a real conflict and must abort. Iceberg retries a few times by default (commit.retry.num-retries is 4) with backoff. The isolation level is snapshot or serializable per table, not across tables.

howItWorks.title: Readers pin a snapshot and prune with stats
howItWorks.text: A query reads the head once and sees that snapshot for its whole life, even while writers commit. The planner prunes partitions and files using manifest stats before opening any data file, which avoids listing the bucket. The same mechanism gives time travel: query an older snapshot by id or timestamp.

howItWorks.title: Maintenance keeps it healthy
howItWorks.text: Streaming writes create many small files, so a compaction job rewrites them to roughly 128 MB to 1 GB each. Old snapshots keep replaced files alive, so you periodically expire snapshots and delete orphan files. Without this, query planning slows down and storage grows without bound.

pros: Atomic, isolated commits on storage that has no transactions of its own
Readers get a consistent snapshot without locking writers
Schema and partition evolution without rewriting the table
Time travel, audit and rollback to an earlier snapshot
Stats in metadata let engines skip files without listing the bucket
Open specs mean Spark, Trino, Flink, Snowflake and DuckDB can share one copy of the data
cons: Every commit is a few object-store round trips, so commit latency is seconds, not milliseconds
Many concurrent writers on one table fight over the same pointer
Needs ongoing maintenance: compaction, snapshot expiry, orphan file cleanup
Row-level updates are expensive compared with a database: they rewrite files or add delete files
Transactions stop at the table boundary; there is no multi-table atomicity in the basic formats
Engine and catalog support for features differs between Iceberg, Delta and Hudi
whenToUse: Analytical data that is large, append-heavy and read by several engines
Streaming or frequent micro-batch ingestion into a table that analysts query
You need reliable reruns, backfills, audit or the ability to roll back a bad load
You want one copy of data shared by warehouse, notebooks and ML jobs instead of exporting copies
whenNotToUse: Transactional workloads with point reads and frequent single-row updates: use a real database
A small dataset (gigabytes) that a single Postgres or a plain Parquet folder serves well
Sub-second end-to-end freshness requirements, since each commit takes seconds and creates small files
A single warehouse already holds and serves all the data and no other engine needs it
pitfalls: Committing every second from many writers: thousands of tiny files, commit conflicts and slow planning
Never running compaction or snapshot expiry, so manifests and storage grow without bound
Expiring snapshots too aggressively while a long query or a time-travel consumer still needs them
Deleting orphan files younger than the longest running write, which removes files a commit is about to reference
Partitioning on a high-cardinality column, which creates millions of tiny partitions
Assuming a file listing is the table: other tools that write to the folder bypass the transaction log
GDPR deletes that only add delete files: the data is still in older files and snapshots until compaction and expiry

roles.label: Writer
roles.description: A batch or streaming job that uploads data files and then tries to commit a new snapshot.

roles.label: Catalog
roles.description: Holds the pointer to the table's current metadata and performs the atomic compare-and-swap.

roles.label: Object store
roles.description: Holds immutable data files, manifests and metadata files, with no transactions of its own.

roles.label: Query engine
roles.description: Reads the head, plans from manifest stats and reads only the files it needs.

quiz.question: Two writers append Parquet files to an object-store folder, and a reader sometimes sees half of a write. The team moves to Apache Iceberg. Why does the reader no longer see partial writes?
options: Iceberg locks the folder while a writer is uploading, so readers wait
New files are not in the table until a commit swaps the pointer
Writers upload to a temporary folder and rename it in one atomic step
Readers retry the file listing until it stops changing
quiz.explanation: Data files are uploaded first but only become part of the table when the catalog pointer moves to the new snapshot, and readers pin one snapshot. Object stores have no atomic multi-file rename, and there is no table-wide lock.

quiz.question: Eight streaming writers commit to one table every 5 seconds. After two weeks queries are slow to plan, and commits keep hitting conflicts. What is the best fix?
options: Partition the table by user id to spread the writers apart
Raise the commit retry count to 20 so conflicts resolve
Run queries against an older snapshot to avoid the new files
Commit in larger batches and schedule compaction and expiry
quiz.explanation: Frequent commits create many tiny files and fight over one pointer. Fewer, larger commits plus compaction and expiry keep planning fast. A high-cardinality partition adds millions of small partitions, and more retries only hide the contention. Reading an older snapshot hides new data but does not fix slow planning or the conflicts.

quiz.question: A nightly job writes data files for up to 3 hours before it commits to an Iceberg table. An operator schedules orphan file removal for files older than 1 hour. What is likely to happen?
options: Time travel queries older than one hour start failing
Compaction can no longer merge the small files in the table
The running job's files are deleted before its commit lands
Readers begin to see partial writes from the running job
quiz.explanation: Uncommitted files look like orphans because no snapshot references them yet. The age threshold must be longer than the longest write. Losing time travel is a snapshot expiry problem, not orphan cleanup, and readers never see uncommitted files, so partial writes are not the risk here.
